title: Heritage walk in Varanasi: the ghats, old city and Sarnath
seo_title: Heritage Walk in Varanasi and Sarnath: Places, Routes, Museums
meta_description: Plan a heritage walk in Varanasi: the ghats, Man Mandir, the old city lanes and Sarnath, a UNESCO site since 2026, with routes, museums and tips for groups.
summary: A heritage walk in Varanasi (Banaras, Kashi) covers the river ghats rebuilt from the 16th to the 19th century, the lanes of the old city, Rajghat where ancient Varanasi was excavated, and Sarnath, 10 km north, where the Buddha gave his first sermon. Sarnath became India's newest UNESCO World Heritage Site in July 2026.

paras: Varanasi is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in South Asia and a major centre of Hindu learning, pilgrimage and death rites. It was the capital of the Kashi mahajanapada in the first millennium BCE, and Buddhist and Jain texts refer to it often. Sarnath, at the city's northern edge, is where the Buddha is said to have taught his first sermon after his enlightenment at Bodh Gaya.

In July 2026 the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan, making it India's 45th World Heritage Site. A walk here therefore joins two different stories: the Buddhist monastic site with its Mauryan and Gupta remains, and the living river city with its ghats, temples and mathas.

Excavations at Rajghat, on a plateau where the Varuna meets the Ganga, show occupation from at least the early first millennium BCE through to the medieval period. The [Indian history timeline](indian-history-timeline.html) places these layers in sequence.

At Sarnath, Ashoka set up a pillar in the 3rd century BCE, with an edict warning against division in the monastic community, topped by the Lion Capital now in the Sarnath Museum and used as India's national emblem. The site grew under the Kushanas and Guptas: the Dhamek Stupa in its present form is usually dated to about the 5th to 6th century CE, and the Sarnath school of Gupta sculpture produced the seated preaching Buddha. The monasteries declined after the 12th century. The [Ashoka and his edicts](ashoka-and-his-edicts.html) guide covers the inscription.

Most of the riverfront you see today was built from the late 16th century onward by Rajput, Maratha and other patrons: Man Singh's palace at Man Mandir Ghat, where Sawai Jai Singh II later added an observatory, and many 18th century Maratha ghats. The present Kashi Vishwanath temple was built in 1780 under Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore, next to the Gyanvapi mosque of Aurangzeb's reign; the relationship between the two sites is the subject of ongoing court proceedings, and a walk treats it historically. Ramnagar Fort across the river dates from the 1750s, and Banaras Hindu University was founded in 1916.

sections.h2: What you see on a walk
paras: On the ghats, look at how each one is a building project with a patron: stairs, platforms, palaces and small shrines built against the river's seasonal rise. At Man Mandir you can compare the observatory instruments with those at Delhi and Jaipur. In the lanes, students see how temples, mathas, houses and markets share a dense old fabric.

At Sarnath, read the plan of monasteries and shrines in brick, the Dharmarajika stupa base, the stump of the Ashokan pillar with its Brahmi edict, and the Dhamek Stupa's carved stone band. A short session on [India's scripts from Brahmi to Sarada](reading-india-s-scripts-brahmi-to-sarada.html) or an [introductory Pali course](pali-a-first-course.html) gives the inscriptions and the early Buddhist texts real meaning.

sections.h2: Varanasi and Sarnath for school and college groups
paras: Groups explore Varanasi through a [study tour built for your group](a-study-tour-built-for-your-group.html). Buddhist archaeology connects well with the [Nalanda monastic university](nalanda-monastic-university-landscape.html) visit in Bihar and with [Sanchi: stupas, gateways and Buddhist art](sanchi-stupas-gateways-and-buddhist-art.html), and families can look at the private journey [Central India: rock art and Buddhist archaeology](central-india-rock-art-and-buddhist-archaeology.html).

The ghats are best walked at dawn, and a boat ride gives the full riverfront in an hour. Manikarnika and Harishchandra are cremation ghats: groups should watch quietly from a distance and not photograph. Sarnath is about 10 km away and needs a vehicle; the site and museum together need half a day. Check ASI rules for the museum, which may restrict photography.

stops.name: Dashashwamedh Ghat
stops.note: The main ghat of the city, with the evening river ritual; start here for the riverfront.

stops.name: Man Mandir Ghat and observatory
stops.note: Man Singh's palace with Sawai Jai Singh II's masonry instruments on the roof.

stops.name: Manikarnika Ghat
stops.note: The main cremation ghat; watch respectfully from a distance and do not photograph.

stops.name: Panchganga Ghat and Alamgir Mosque
stops.note: Ghat with a mosque of Aurangzeb's reign built above the stairs.

stops.name: Kashi Vishwanath Temple
stops.note: Temple rebuilt under Ahilyabai Holkar, now reached through a new corridor from the river.

stops.name: Assi Ghat
stops.note: Southern end of the ghats, near the confluence of the Assi stream.

stops.name: Rajghat
stops.note: Plateau at the Varuna confluence where excavations found the ancient city.

stops.name: Ramnagar Fort
stops.note: Fort of the Maharajas of Banaras on the east bank, with a museum of the royal collection.

stops.name: Banaras Hindu University
stops.note: Campus with Bharat Kala Bhavan museum and the New Vishwanath temple.

stops.name: Dhamek Stupa
stops.note: Cylindrical stupa at Sarnath with a band of carved floral and geometric stone.

stops.name: Dharmarajika Stupa and Ashokan pillar
stops.note: Base of a stupa linked to Ashoka and the stump of his inscribed pillar.

stops.name: Mulagandhakuti ruins
stops.note: Remains of the main shrine and monastery blocks, laid out in brick.

stops.name: Chaukhandi Stupa
stops.note: Brick stupa marking where the Buddha met his first disciples, with an octagonal tower added under Akbar.

stops.name: Sarnath Museum
stops.note: The ASI's oldest site museum, home of the Ashokan Lion Capital and the Gupta preaching Buddha.

routes.name: The ghats at dawn
routes.length: About 2 to 3 hours on foot, or a boat

routes.name: Sarnath
routes.length: Half a day, by vehicle from the city

museums.name: Sarnath Museum
museums.note: The Lion Capital, the seated preaching Buddha and Gupta sculpture from the site.

museums.name: Bharat Kala Bhavan, BHU
museums.note: University museum with sculpture, miniature paintings, textiles and Banaras material.

museums.name: Ramnagar Fort museum
museums.note: Royal collection of the Maharajas of Banaras: palanquins, arms, costumes and clocks.

best_time: October to March. Walk the ghats at dawn; in the monsoon the river rises over many ghats.

faq.q: Is Sarnath a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faq.a: Yes. The Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath was inscribed in July 2026 at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan. It is India's 45th World Heritage Site.

faq.q: Which historical places in Varanasi are best for a heritage walk?
faq.a: The ghats from Assi to Panchganga, Man Mandir with its observatory, the old city around Kashi Vishwanath, Rajghat, Ramnagar Fort and, 10 km away, Sarnath with the Dhamek Stupa and the Sarnath Museum.

faq.q: Is a Varanasi heritage walk suitable for schools?
faq.a: Yes, with care. Walk the ghats at dawn in small groups, keep away from the cremation ghats, and spend half a day at Sarnath, which is open, quiet and easy to manage with a class.

faq.q: What are the main museums in Varanasi?
faq.a: The Sarnath Museum, with the Ashokan Lion Capital; Bharat Kala Bhavan at Banaras Hindu University; and the Ramnagar Fort museum across the river.

faq.q: Can a Varanasi and Sarnath visit be arranged for our group?
faq.a: Yes. Talaash Heritage arranges study tours to Varanasi and Sarnath on request, with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi, for schools, colleges, companies and private groups.
